title: netgraph element document
description: One netgraph element declared in YAML, `apiVersion: netgraph.dev/v1alpha1`. This schema is versioned with that apiVersion: it describes structure, value grammars and the cross-field rules of a single object. Rules that span documents — that a cable endpoint resolves, that names are unique, that an address is inside its subnet — are checked by `netgraph validate`.

Adapter.description: A device presenting network interfaces over a non-network host port.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. Presents interfaces over a non-network host port.

Adapter.title: Adapter

serial.title: serial
serial.description: Serial or asset number, free text.

form_factor.title: form_factor
form_factor.description: What sort of adapter this is: `usb-ethernet`, `dock`, `media-converter`, `sfp-module`. Descriptive only.

passthrough.title: passthrough
passthrough.description: May the renderer collapse the adapter into its host? True draws the host and the adapter as one node at layer 2; false keeps them separate.

ports.title: ports
ports.description: How many downstream ports the hardware physically has. Declaring it lets the validator catch an inventory that outgrew the device (`E006`).

upstream.title: upstream
upstream.description: The host-facing port: the bus the adapter plugs into.

interfaces.title: interfaces
interfaces.description:
The network ports the adapter presents downstream. Only `ethernet`, `wifi` and `lag` are allowed (`NG-X003`).

YANG: `/if:interfaces/if:interface`

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

AddressFamily.description:
Which of the two protocol families a policy rule is installed in.

The policy database is per family — an IPv4 rule and an IPv6 rule with the
same priority are two rules, in two lists, that never see each other's
packets. Most rules say which family they are in by carrying a prefix; the
field is for the ones that do not, and the one place it is *not* optional is
a reader's understanding.
AddressFamily.title: AddressFamily

AnnotationGeometry.description:
Where an annotation is drawn, and how big it is.

Flat rather than the nested ``position``/``size`` of §18, because these four
numbers are what a drag and a resize produce and what an editor writes back;
a note is one box, not a node with an optional extent.

Coordinates are the §18 system: points, ``y`` upwards, and ``x``/``y`` is
the **centre** of the box. Both or neither: half a position places nothing.
AnnotationGeometry.title: AnnotationGeometry

Area.description: A ``kind: area`` document: one zone drawn behind the diagram.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. A labelled box drawn behind the nodes, enclosing the elements it names, matches or encircles. The declarative form of `--collapse` grouping: the same set of elements, boxed rather than folded.

spec.title: spec
spec.description: The body of an `area` document: which elements the zone encloses, and how the box round them is drawn.

Area.title: Area

AreaSelector.description:
Which elements an area contains, said as a query rather than a list.

Every clause that is given must match, and a selector with no clause at all
is refused: it would silently box the entire inventory.
AreaSelector.title: AreaSelector

AreaSpec.description: A labelled region drawn behind the nodes.
AreaSpec.title: AreaSpec

Assertion.description: One claim about the network, and everything needed to grade it (§20.2).
Assertion.title: Assertion

AssertionLayer.description: Which view of the network an assertion is made about.
AssertionLayer.title: AssertionLayer

AssertionType.description: What an assertion claims. The value is the word written in ``assert``.
AssertionType.title: AssertionType

Band.description:
§6.2.6 — the three bands 802.11 operates in.

The band is not derivable from the channel number: channels 1 to 13 exist in
both the 2.4 GHz and the 6 GHz plan and mean different frequencies, so a
document that states a channel has to state the band with it (`NG-W003`).
Band.title: Band

BgpConfig.description: `spec.routing.bgp` — the local AS, its router id and its neighbours.

asn.title: asn
asn.description: Local autonomous system number, 1 to 4294967295. AS 0 is reserved (RFC 7607).

router_id.title: router_id
router_id.description: BGP identifier — a dotted quad. Unique across the inventory (`NG-F012`); commonly the same value as the OSPF router id, which is one identity rather than a duplicate.

neighbors.title: neighbors
neighbors.description: The sessions this device configures. Peers are named by address, never by element name.

BgpConfig.title: BgpConfig

BgpNeighbor.description:
One entry of `spec.routing.bgp.neighbors` — a configured session.

The peer is an **address**, not a name. That is what the device is
configured with, and it is what lets the graph layer find the peer among the
addresses the inventory already declares without a second reference grammar
that could point somewhere else (§16.6).

address.title: address
address.description: Peer address. Resolved against every address the inventory configures; a peer that resolves to nothing is `NG-F013`, a warning, because an eBGP peer may be external.

remote_asn.title: remote_asn
remote_asn.description: The AS the peer is in. Checked against the peer's own `asn` when the address resolves (`NG-F011`).

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the session is for.

BgpNeighbor.title: BgpNeighbor

name.title: name
name.description:
Name of the bridge component. Defaults to `metadata.name` once the document is loaded.

YANG: `/dot1q:bridges/dot1q:bridge/dot1q:name`

type.title: type
type.description:
802.1Q bridge type, which decides the `dot1q:port-type` of every port on the device.

YANG: `/dot1q:bridges/dot1q:bridge/dot1q:bridge-type`

anyOf.title: MAC address
anyOf.description: An EUI-48 address in colon (`00:1e:8c:00:10:01`), dash (`00-1E-8C-00-10-01`) or Cisco dotted (`001e.8c00.1001`) form, normalised to lower-case colon form on load. Quote it: an unquoted MAC can be read as a number by a YAML 1.1 parser.

address.title: address
address.description:
Bridge address (the bridge's own MAC), used as the spanning-tree bridge identifier.

YANG: `/dot1q:bridges/dot1q:bridge/dot1q:address`

Bss.description:
One entry of `interfaces[].wireless.bss` — a basic service set.

On an `ap` radio each entry is an SSID the radio beacons, with the VLAN
its traffic is bridged into. On a `station` or `mesh` radio the single
entry names the BSS the radio is associated to, which is what `NG-W010`
checks against the AP at the other end of the link.

ssid.title: ssid
ssid.description:
The network name, 1 to 32 octets. Unique within one radio (`NG-W005`), and on a client radio it must be one the AP at the far end advertises (`NG-W010`).

YANG: `…/dot11:bss/dot11:ssid`

bssid.title: bssid
bssid.description:
MAC address of this BSS — usually the radio's own for the first SSID and a derived one for each further SSID. Unique across the inventory (`NG-W008`).

YANG: `…/dot11:bss/dot11:bssid`

vlan.title: vlan
vlan.description: The VLAN this SSID's traffic is bridged into. Absent means the radio's untagged domain. Checked against the device's VLAN database (`W113`) and against the VLANs the access point actually carries (`NG-W009`).

security.title: security
security.description:
How the BSS authenticates: `open`, or WPA2/WPA3 with a passphrase (`-psk`) or an authentication server (`-eap`). Absent means nobody recorded it.

YANG: `…/dot11:bss/dot11:rsna-enabled`

hidden.title: hidden
hidden.description: The SSID is left out of the beacon. It is still on the air, and still a BSS this radio serves.

Bss.title: Bss

Cable.description: An undirected physical link between exactly two interfaces.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. An undirected link between exactly two interfaces. Owns no interfaces.

Cable.title: Cable

endpoints.title: endpoints
endpoints.description: Exactly two `device:interface` references (`NG-C001`). The link is undirected, so the pair is sorted on load and the order carries no meaning.

medium.title: medium
medium.description: What the link physically is. `wireless` requires both endpoints to be `type: wifi` and forbids `length_m` and `category` (`NG-C006`, `NG-C007`).

anyOf.title: Bit rate
anyOf.description: A link rate, either a whole number of bit/s or `<number><unit>` with unit `bps`, `kbps`, `Mbps`, `Gbps` or `Tbps` (`1Gbps`). Stored in bit/s.

speed.title: speed
speed.description:
Negotiated link rate. Written as bit/s or as `1Gbps`; stored in bit/s. Projected onto `if:speed` of both endpoints, which is `config false`.

YANG: `…/if:speed (on both endpoints)`

duplex.title: duplex
duplex.description: Duplex of the link. `half` outside a hub link is `NG-C013`.

length_m.title: length_m
length_m.description: Physical length in metres. Documentation only.

label.title: label
label.description: The identifier printed on the cable or the patch panel. Drawn on the edge.

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

Computer.description: An end host, drawn as a workstation.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. End host, drawn as a workstation.

Computer.title: Computer

ConnState.description:
A connection-tracking state (`ct state` / `conntrack --ctstate`).

The reason a modern ruleset is short: one rule accepting `established` and
`related` replaces the return path of every other rule in the file, and a
document that could not say so would have to describe both directions of
every flow.
ConnState.title: ConnState

vendor.title: vendor
vendor.description: Hardware vendor, free text. Documentation only.

serial.title: serial
serial.description: Serial or asset number, free text.

location.title: location
location.description: Physical location, free text (site, room, rack unit).

interfaces.title: interfaces
interfaces.description:
Every port and logical interface the device owns. At least one is required.

YANG: `/if:interfaces/if:interface`

bridge.title: bridge
bridge.description:
The 802.1Q bridge component this device implements. Absent means the device is not a bridge.

YANG: `/dot1q:bridges/dot1q:bridge`

vlans.title: vlans
vlans.description:
The device VLAN database: which VLANs exist on this device, and what they are called.

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-vlan/dot1q:vlan`

forwarding.title: forwarding
forwarding.description: Device-wide default for per-interface IP forwarding. Defaults to true/true on a `router` and false/false on every other kind; a `hub` must not declare it.

netns.title: netns
netns.description: The network namespaces this machine runs (§23.1). Each is a whole second network stack — its own interfaces, addresses and routing table — and `parent` nests one inside another, arbitrarily deep. Not a VRF: a VRF partitions one stack's routing table, a namespace *is* a second stack.

vrfs.title: vrfs
vrfs.description:
The routing instances (VRFs) this device implements. An interface binds to one with `vrf`, and that binding is what partitions the address namespace.

YANG: `/ni:network-instances/ni:network-instance`

route_tables.title: route_tables
route_tables.description: The routing tables this device holds beyond `main`, `local` and `default`. A table on its own changes nothing; what reaches it is a rule in `routing_policy` (§16.4).

routes.title: routes
routes.description:
Configured static routes, in the order the device holds them.

YANG: `…/rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/rt:control-plane-protocol/rt:static-routes`

routing_policy.title: routing_policy
routing_policy.description: The routing policy database: the ordered rules deciding which *table* a packet is routed by, from its source, its firewall mark, its ingress interface or its DSCP. This is policy-based routing (§16.4).

routing.title: routing
routing.description:
The dynamic routing protocols the device takes part in: an OSPF area, a BGP autonomous system, or both.

YANG: `…/rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/rt:control-plane-protocol`

zones.title: zones
zones.description: The security zones the device divides its interfaces into (§24.1). Policy is written *between* zones rather than between interfaces, so a rule survives a port being renamed, doubled or moved to a LAG. An interface is in at most one zone (`NG-B003`).

firewall.title: firewall
firewall.description: What the device does to the packets it sees: the filter policy and the address translations (§24.2). Absent records nothing about its filtering, which is not the same as saying it filters nothing.

power.title: power
power.description:
What the device draws, which PDU outlets feed it, and how much PoE it hands out (§17.2). Absent means the inventory records nothing about its power.

YANG: `/eo-mib:eoPowerTable/eoPowerEntry`

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

from.title: from
from.description: Names a `kind: template` document whose partial spec is merged underneath this one. The device's own keys win; `interfaces` merge by `name`; any other list the device declares replaces the template's outright. Resolved with the ordinary reference rules, so a template may live in another namespace (`templates/c9200l-48p`).

EdgeGeometry.description:
How one link is drawn: its bends, its routing style and its label.

The waypoints are the **interior** points of the route, in the order
written, from the ``source`` end to the ``target`` end of the edge as the
graph orders them; the two ends are the nodes, which is why moving a node
moves the route without invalidating the bends. An entry carrying none of
the three fields is refused (``NG-Y003``): it says nothing, and the way to
say nothing is to leave the key out.
EdgeGeometry.title: EdgeGeometry

Firewall.description:
A layer-3 forwarder that filters. Forwards by default (§6.1.1).

Structurally a router, and deliberately so: the `spec` is the same one,
because the difference between a firewall and a router is a policy either of
them may carry rather than a shape only one of them has. `spec.zones` and
`spec.firewall` are available on every layer-3 kind (§24), so a router with
three rules on it is describable — which it has to be, since that is what
most networks actually run.

What the kind buys is the picture and the vocabulary. An operator who bought
a box whose whole job is filtering writes `kind: firewall` and gets a brick
wall on the diagram rather than a router's diamond, and every reader of the
inventory learns at a glance which boxes the policy is expected to be on.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. A router that filters. Forwards by default; drawn as a wall. Structurally identical to `router` — `zones` and `firewall` are available on every layer-3 kind.

Firewall.title: Firewall

FirewallAction.description:
What happens to a packet a filter rule matches.

Three of the five *decide* the packet's fate and end the walk; two of them
do something to it and let the walk continue. That split is the whole reason
the list is not simply "accept or drop": a rule that logs and a rule that
marks are useful precisely because the packet carries on to the rule that
decides, and a schema in which every action terminated could express neither.
FirewallAction.title: FirewallAction

FirewallConfig.description:
`spec.firewall` — what the device does to the packets it sees (§24.2).

The three defaults are what happens to a packet no rule decided, one per
hook, and they are stated rather than left implicit because they are the most
consequential three words in any ruleset. They default to *deny inbound,
deny transit, permit outbound*: the shape every firewall guide has recommended
for thirty years, and the one whose failure mode is a service that does not
work rather than a network that is open.

default_input.title: default_input
default_input.description: What a packet *for this machine* gets when no rule decides. One of `accept`, `drop` and `reject` — a default has to decide (`NG-B007`). Defaults to `drop`.

default_forward.title: default_forward
default_forward.description: What a packet *through* this machine gets when no rule decides, on the same terms. Defaults to `drop`.

default_output.title: default_output
default_output.description: What a packet *from* this machine gets when no rule decides, on the same terms. Defaults to `accept`: a machine that cannot answer a DNS query cannot be administered either.

rules.title: rules
rules.description: The filter policy, in declaration order. What the device walks is this list in *priority* order, lowest first, first terminal match deciding (§24.2).

nat.title: nat
nat.description: The address translations, in the order they are tried (§24.4). Apart from `rules` because a packet is translated *and* filtered, in different hooks.

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the policy as a whole is for.

FirewallConfig.title: FirewallConfig

FirewallRule.description:
One entry of `spec.firewall.rules` — a filter rule (§24.2).

Read it as a sentence: *at priority 100, a TCP packet from the lan zone to
this machine's port 22 is accepted*. The zones and the selectors are the
subject, the action is the verb, and `priority` is where in the queue the
sentence is read — lowest first, first terminal match wins.

A rule that names no zone and no selector matches every packet, which is not
a mistake: it is how a chain is terminated. It is also how a chain is broken,
by numbering a rule above the terminator instead of below it, which is
`W154`.

priority.title: priority
priority.description: Unique within the device, per family (`NG-B008`). The chain is walked from the lowest priority upwards; the first rule whose action is terminal decides, and nothing after it is consulted.

name.title: name
name.description: Optional label, for the diagram and for a diagnostic to name the rule by.

src_zone.title: src_zone
src_zone.description: The zone the packet came from: a declared zone, or `local` for traffic this machine generated (`NG-B004`). Unset matches any zone.

dst_zone.title: dst_zone
dst_zone.description: The zone the packet is going to, on the same terms (`NG-B004`). Together with `src_zone` this decides the hook: `to: local` is input, `from: local` is output, two real zones are forward.

family.title: family
family.description: Which family's chain the rule is in. Omit to install in both, and derive from `src`, `dst` or `protocol` when possible (`NG-B005`); `ipv4` and `ipv6` are explicit.

src.title: src
src.description: Source prefix selector. Either family; optional.

dst.title: dst
dst.description: Destination prefix selector, on the same terms.

protocol.title: protocol
protocol.description: The IP protocol. Required by `src_ports` and `dst_ports`, which only `tcp`, `udp` and `sctp` have (`NG-B005`). `icmp` is IPv4 and `icmpv6` is IPv6, and stating one against the other family is refused.

src_ports.title: src_ports
src_ports.description: Source ports: single ports and closed ranges (`443`, `30000-32767`), matched as a set.

dst_ports.title: dst_ports
dst_ports.description: Destination ports, on the same terms. The usual selector, since it is the one that names the service.

ct_state.title: ct_state
ct_state.description: Connection-tracking states, matched as a set. Empty matches any state; one rule accepting `established` and `related` replaces the return path of every other rule.

iif.title: iif
iif.description: Ingress interface selector (`NG-B009`), for when a zone is too coarse. Rare: the point of a zone is not needing this.

oif.title: oif
oif.description: Egress interface selector, on the same terms (`NG-B009`).

invert.title: invert
invert.description: Match everything the selectors do not. Meaningless without a selector to invert (`NG-B005`).

action.title: action
action.description: `accept`, `drop` and `reject` decide the packet and end the walk; `mark` writes a firewall mark and `log` records it, and both carry on to the next rule. Stated, never defaulted.

mark.title: mark
mark.description: The mark to write, hexadecimal, optionally masked. Required by `action: mark` and refused by everything else (`NG-B005`). This is what `spec.routing_policy[].fwmark` reads — see §16.9 and §24.3.

log_prefix.title: log_prefix
log_prefix.description: The tag put in front of a logged packet. For `action: log` only (`NG-B005`).

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the rule is for.

FirewallRule.title: FirewallRule

ipv4.description:
Default for `interfaces[].ipv4.forwarding` on this device.

YANG: `…/ip:ipv4/ip:forwarding (as the default)`

ipv6.title: ipv6
ipv6.description:
Default for `interfaces[].ipv6.forwarding` on this device.

YANG: `…/ip:ipv6/ip:forwarding (as the default)`

Group.description: A named set of identities, which may hold other groups (§19.2).

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. A named set of identities. `members` may name a `user` or another `group`, which is what makes a hierarchy expressible; the nesting must not loop (`NG-S012`).

Group.title: Group

GroupGeometry.description:
The box one namespace cluster is drawn as.

Unlike a node, a group carries a required :attr:`size`: nothing else decides
how big it is, because a cluster is drawn around whatever the arrangement
put inside it rather than around whatever Graphviz packed into it.
GroupGeometry.title: GroupGeometry

members.title: members
members.description: The users and nested groups in this group, as element references resolved outwards from the group's own namespace. Must resolve (`NG-S010`), must be an identity (`NG-S011`), and the nesting must not loop (`NG-S012`).

gid.title: gid
gid.description: POSIX group id, when the estate assigns one. 0 to 4294967294; two groups claiming one is `NG-S013`.

email.title: email
email.description: Where mail to the whole group goes, when the group is also a distribution list.

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

Hub.description: A layer-1 repeater: no MAC table, no VLANs, no IP stack (§6.5).

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. Layer-1 repeater. Rejects `vlan`, `ipv4`, `ipv6`, `bridge`, `vlans` and `forwarding`; every interface must be `ethernet`.

Hub.title: Hub

IPv4Address.title: IPv4 address
IPv4Address.description: One IPv4 address, written as `10.0.0.1/24` or as a mapping with `ip` and either `prefix_length` or `netmask`.

netmask.title: netmask
netmask.description: The dotted-quad spelling of `prefix_length`, normalised away on load. Mutually exclusive with `prefix_length`; a non-contiguous mask is rejected (`NG-A003`).

IPv4Config.title: IPv4 configuration
IPv4Config.description: The RFC 8344 `ip:ipv4` container. A bare list of addresses is shorthand for `{addresses: [...]}`.

IPv6Address.title: IPv6 address
IPv6Address.description: One IPv6 address, written as `2001:db8::1/64` or as a mapping with `ip` and `prefix_length`. Quote it if it would otherwise start a YAML alias or flow mapping.

IPv6Config.title: IPv6 configuration
IPv6Config.description: The RFC 8344 `ip:ipv6` container. A bare list of addresses is shorthand for `{addresses: [...]}`.

InterfaceRef.title: Interface reference
InterfaceRef.description: A reference to one port, written as `device:interface`. The device half may be fully qualified (`sites/berlin/rack1/sw1:eth0`) to pick one of several elements sharing a short name. The mapping form `{device: ..., interface: ...}` is equivalent.

InterfaceType.description: §6.2.1 — the four core types plus the three extension types.
InterfaceType.title: InterfaceType

LabelGeometry.description:
Where a link's annotation sits, relative to the link.

Stored *on the link* rather than as a coordinate, so that nudging a VLAN
label clear of a crossing cable survives both endpoints being dragged
somewhere else. :attr:`at` slides it along the route and :attr:`offset`
lifts it off, in points, in the same ``y``-upwards system as everything
else here.
LabelGeometry.title: LabelGeometry

Layout.description: A ``kind: layout`` document: geometry for one or more views.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. Diagram geometry for elements declared elsewhere, scoped by view. Not an element: it carries no network facts and is never drawn as a node. See `netgraph layout`.

spec.title: spec
spec.description: The body of a `layout` document: one arrangement per view.

Layout.title: Layout

LayoutSpec.description: The arrangements one layout document carries, one per view.

Legend.description: A ``kind: legend`` document: one key on the diagram.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. A key: what the colours and line styles of the drawing mean, placed by corner rather than by coordinate. `auto: layers` derives the entries from what the view drew.

spec.title: spec
spec.description: The body of a `legend` document: the key, and which corner it sits in.

Legend.title: Legend

LegendEntry.description: One row of a key: a swatch and what it means.
LegendEntry.title: LegendEntry

LegendSpec.description: A key: what the colours and the line styles in this drawing mean.
LegendSpec.title: LegendSpec

Location.description:
`metadata.location` — where the hardware physically is (§3.2).

Free-text `spec.location` says it in prose, which is enough for a label
and useless for anything else: no tool can tell from `"MDF, third rack,
near the top"` whether two things collide. This block is the structured
form, and it is on `metadata` rather than on a `spec` because it is true
of every kind — a patch panel is racked exactly as a server is.

`position` is the *lowest* rack unit the element occupies and `height`
how many it takes, so a 2U server at `position: 10` fills U10 and U11.
Units count from 1 at the bottom, which is how a cabinet is labelled.

site.title: site
site.description: Site the element is installed at, free text.

room.title: room
room.description: Room or floor within the site, free text.

rack.title: rack
rack.description: Rack identifier, unique within its room. Naming one is what puts the element on an elevation; site, room and rack together identify the rack (`NG-U001`).

position.title: position

rack_height.title: rack_height
rack_height.description: How tall the rack itself is. Any element in the rack may declare it; two that disagree are `NG-U003`, and nothing may extend past it (`NG-U002`).

location.title: location
location.description: Where the hardware physically is: site, room, rack and the rack units it occupies. Drives `--layer rack` and the placement rules `NG-U001` to `NG-U004`.

NatRule.description:
One entry of `spec.firewall.nat` — an address translation (§24.4).

Apart from the filter rules because it happens apart from them: a packet is
translated *and* filtered, in different hooks, and a list that mixed the two
would have to answer which happened first for every pair of entries in it.

Order within the list is the order the translations are tried, first match
winning, which is what every implementation does. There is no `priority`:
a NAT list is short enough that its own order is readable, and a number that
only ever repeated the position would be one more thing to keep in step.

name.title: name
name.description: Optional label, for a diagnostic to name the translation by.

type.title: type
type.description: `snat` and `masquerade` rewrite the source on the way out; `dnat` and `redirect` rewrite the destination on the way in. Which of the two fields below are required follows from this (`NG-B006`).

src_zone.title: src_zone
src_zone.description: The zone the packet came from (`NG-B004`).

dst_zone.title: dst_zone
dst_zone.description: The zone it is going to (`NG-B004`). The usual selector for a source translation: *everything leaving towards the wan is masqueraded*.

family.title: family
family.description: Which family the translation is in. Derived from any address it names (`NG-B006`).

dst_ports.title: dst_ports
dst_ports.description: Destination ports: the *published* port, not the internal one, which is `to_port`.

to_address.title: to_address
to_address.description: What the address becomes. Required by `snat` and `dnat`; refused by `masquerade` (whose address is the egress interface's, unknown here) and by `redirect` (whose address is this machine) — `NG-B006`.

to_port.title: to_port
to_port.description: What the port becomes. Required by `redirect`, which translates the port and nothing else; on a source translation it needs a `dst_ports` to be about (`NG-B006`).

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the translation is for.

NatRule.title: NatRule

NatType.description: Which address a NAT rule rewrites, and on which side of the machine.
NatType.title: NatType

NetnsDefinition.description:
One entry of `spec.netns` — a network namespace on the device (§23.1).

Three fields and no configuration: everything a namespace *contains* is
declared by the things that name it. Interfaces move into one with
`interfaces[].netns`, and that is also what gives the namespace its
addresses and its routes, because those hang off the interfaces.

`NG-N020` (names are unique per device), `NG-N021` (`parent` resolves
and does not loop) and `NG-N022` (`interfaces[].netns` resolves) are all
checked by the device spec, where the whole table is in view.

name.title: name
name.description: Name of the namespace, as `ip netns` spells it. Unique within the device (`NG-N020`), and what `interfaces[].netns` and another entry's `parent` refer to.

parent.title: parent
parent.description: The namespace this one was created inside (`NG-N021`). Unset means the machine's initial namespace. This is the whole of the hierarchy: a namespace has exactly one creator, so nesting is a tree.

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the namespace is for — a tenant, a container, a test harness.

OspfConfig.description:
`spec.routing.ospf` — one OSPF area and the interfaces that run it.

One area per device, deliberately: an area border router is a real thing,
but modelling it needs per-interface areas, and a single area covers the
inventories this revision is for. See §16.7.

area.title: area
area.description: Area identifier, written as a dotted quad or as a plain number; `0` and `0.0.0.0` are the same backbone area and both normalise to `0.0.0.0`.

router_id.title: router_id
router_id.description: Router identifier — a dotted quad even in an IPv6-only network. Unique across the inventory (`NG-F012`).

interfaces.title: interfaces
interfaces.description:
The interfaces OSPF runs on. Non-empty, free of duplicates (`NG-F006`), and each one an interface of this device (`NG-F010`).

YANG: `/if:interfaces/if:interface/if:name`

OspfConfig.title: OspfConfig

PartialInterface.description: One interface, with only its identity required. This is the shape an entry takes inside a `spec` that inherits a template: the device restates the `name` and the handful of fields it overrides, and the template supplies the rest. Everywhere else `type` is required too — see `Interface`.

name.title: name
name.description:
Interface name as the device itself spells it (`eth0`, `GigabitEthernet0/2`). Unique within the element (`NG-I001`), and the target of a cable endpoint.

YANG: `/if:interfaces/if:interface/if:name`

type.title: type
type.description:
What kind of interface this is. Decides which other fields are allowed and whether a cable may terminate here (`NG-C009`).

YANG: `…/if:type`

description.title: description
description.description:
Free text describing what the port is for.

YANG: `…/if:description`

enabled.title: enabled
enabled.description:
Intended administrative state. A disabled interface is exempt from `W101`.

YANG: `…/if:enabled`

anyOf.title: MAC address
anyOf.description: An EUI-48 address in colon (`00:1e:8c:00:10:01`), dash (`00-1E-8C-00-10-01`) or Cisco dotted (`001e.8c00.1001`) form, normalised to lower-case colon form on load. Quote it: an unquoted MAC can be read as a number by a YAML 1.1 parser.

mac.title: mac
mac.description:
Hardware address, EUI-48. Accepted in colon, dash or Cisco dotted form and normalised to lower-case colon form. `if:phys-address` is `config false` in RFC 8343, so an exporter must not write it to a live datastore.

YANG: `…/if:phys-address`

mtu.title: mtu
mtu.description: Layer-2 MTU in bytes. Propagated to `ipv4.mtu` and `ipv6.mtu` when those are not set. RFC 8343 has no layer-2 MTU node.

ipv4.title: ipv4
ipv4.description:
IPv4 configuration. Absent means the interface has no IPv4 stack.

YANG: `…/ip:ipv4`

ipv6.title: ipv6
ipv6.description:
IPv6 configuration. Absent means the interface has no IPv6 stack.

YANG: `…/ip:ipv6`

vlan.title: vlan
vlan.description:
802.1Q bridge-port configuration. Absent means the port is not VLAN-aware; a host port facing an access port normally omits it.

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-port`

vrf.title: vrf
vrf.description:
The routing instance this interface is in. Names an entry of the device's `spec.vrfs` (`NG-F002`); unset means the global instance. An address only collides with another address in the same VRF.

YANG: `/ni:network-instances/ni:network-instance/ni:name`

wireless.title: wireless
wireless.description:
Radio configuration of a `type: wifi` interface: which side of the association it is, which frequency it uses and which BSSs it beacons or joins. Forbidden on every other type (`NG-W002`).

YANG: `…/dot11:wireless-interface`

poe.title: poe
poe.description:
This port is power sourcing equipment: it hands power down the cable (§17.3). Only on a type a cable terminates on — `ethernet` or `lag` (`NG-E006`).

YANG: `/power-ethernet-mib:pethPsePortTable/pethPsePortEntry`

parent.title: parent
parent.description:
The interface this one is stacked on. Required for `type: vlan`, forbidden otherwise (`NG-I002`).

YANG: `…/if:lower-layer-if`

members.title: members
members.description:
The interfaces aggregated by this one. Required for `type: lag` and `type: bridge`, forbidden otherwise (`NG-I003`).

YANG: `…/if:lower-layer-if`

netns.title: netns
netns.description: The network namespace this interface lives in (§23.1). Names an entry of the device's `spec.netns` (`NG-N022`); unset means the machine's initial namespace. Unlike `vrf`, which partitions one stack's routing table, this places the interface in a different stack entirely — its addresses do not collide with the same addresses elsewhere on the machine.

peer.title: peer
peer.description:
The other end of the veth pair this interface is one end of (§23.2). Names another `type: ethernet` interface of the same element, which must name this one back (`NG-N023`). A veth end is `ianaift:ethernetCsmacd` like any other port; what it has instead of a socket is this peer, so a cable must not terminate on it (`NG-N024`).

YANG: `…/if:lower-layer-if`

range.title: range
range.description: Declares many interfaces at once instead of `name`, by bracket expansion over one or more numeric spans: `GigabitEthernet1/0/[1-48]`, `ge-[0-1]/0/[0-3]`. Several spans expand as an odometer, rightmost fastest; the width of the low bound is the zero padding (`[01-12]` yields `01`…`12`). In `description`, `{}` and `%d` stand for the last span and `{0}`, `{1}`, … for a span by position. The loader expands the entry before anything else sees the document, so a range never reaches validation, the graph or a renderer.

kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. A passive cross-connect. Its `front/<n>` and `rear/<n>` ports are derived from `ports`, and a coupler joins each front port to one rear port; it is not a hop.

couplers.title: couplers

outlets.description:

YANG: `/entity-mib:entPhysicalTable/entPhysicalEntry`

capacity_watts.title: capacity_watts
capacity_watts.description:

YANG: `/eo-mib:eoPowerTable/eoPowerEntry/eoPowerNameplate`

input_feed.title: input_feed
input_feed.description:
Which supply feeds the unit — `A`, `B`, `ups-1`, `utility`. Free text, compared only for equality: two PDUs on one feed do not make a device redundant (`NG-E015`).

YANG: `/eo-ctx-mib:eoPowerRelationTable/eoPowerRelationEntry`

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

PoeConfig.description:
`interfaces[].poe` — this port is a PSE (§17.3).

Declaring the block is what makes the port a power sourcing equipment port;
`enabled: false` records a port that *could* source power and is
administratively told not to, which is `pethPsePortAdminEnable` and is the
difference between "no PoE here" and "PoE turned off here".

How much the port reserves is said in one of two ways, and never both
(`NG-E004`):

* `class` — an IEEE classification. The reservation is the PSE-side figure
  for that class (:data:`POE_PSE_WATTS`), which is what the switch actually
  takes out of its budget.
* `budget_watts` — an explicit reservation, for a vendor that lets an
  operator cap a port below its class.

With neither, the port reserves its standard's maximum: that is what a switch
with no per-port configuration does, and assuming less would make an
oversubscribed budget look fine.

standard.title: standard
standard.description:
Which IEEE 802.3 amendment the port implements: `802.3af` (classes 0-3), `802.3at` (adds 4) or `802.3bt` (adds 5-8).

YANG: `/power-ethernet-mib:pethPsePortTable/pethPsePortEntry/pethPsePortType`

class.title: class
class.description:
The IEEE classification, 0 to 8, written `class` in YAML. Fixes the reservation; refused above the standard's own ceiling, and exclusive with `budget_watts` (`NG-E004`).

YANG: `…/pethPsePortEntry/pethPsePortPowerClassifications`

budget_watts.title: budget_watts
budget_watts.description:
An explicit reservation in watts instead of a class, for a vendor that lets an operator cap a port below what its class allows.

YANG: `…/pethPsePortEntry/pethPsePortPowerLimit`

enabled.title: enabled
enabled.description:
Is the port administratively allowed to source power? A disabled PSE port reserves nothing and powers nothing, which is what `NG-E014` reports it for.

YANG: `…/pethPsePortEntry/pethPsePortAdminEnable`

PoeConfig.title: PoeConfig

PoeStandard.description: Which IEEE 802.3 amendment a PSE port implements (§17.3).
PoeStandard.title: PoeStandard

Point.description: A position in points, ``y`` upwards, origin at the bottom left.
Point.title: Point

PolicyAction.description:
What happens to a packet a policy rule matches.

`lookup` is the rule that does the routing; the other four are the ones
that stop it, and they exist because a policy database without them can only
ever *add* reachability. A rule that discards traffic from a guest prefix is
one line here and a firewall in its absence.
PolicyAction.title: PolicyAction

PolicyRule.description:
One entry of `spec.routing_policy` — a rule of the policy database (§16.4).

Read it as a sentence, which is how every implementation writes it: *at
priority 100, a packet from 10.20.0.0/16 is routed by the table called
uplink-b*. The selectors are the subject, the action is the verb, and the
`priority` is where in the queue the sentence is read — lowest first, first
match wins, and nothing after a matching `lookup` is consulted.

The selectors are all layer 3 or below on purpose (see the module docstring):
where the packet came from, where it is going, which interface it arrived on
or would leave by, what the firewall marked it with, and what it asked for in
its DSCP. A rule that names none of them matches everything, which is not a
mistake — it is how the database is terminated.

priority.title: priority
priority.description: Where the rule sits in the policy database, 0-4294967295. The database is walked from the lowest priority upwards and the first match decides, so this is the rule's position and its identity: unique within the device per family (`NG-F020`).

family.title: family
family.description: `ipv4` or `ipv6` — which family's database the rule is installed in. Derived from `src`/`dst` when they say, and both families when nothing does.

src.title: src
src.description: Match packets from this prefix. The selector policy-based routing exists for: it is what makes a source route a source route.

anyOf.description: A mark, with an optional mask: `0x1`, `0x1/0xff`, `1/255`.
The same mark as a plain number, normalised to hexadecimal.

fwmark.title: fwmark
fwmark.description: Match the mark a firewall put on the packet, optionally masked: `0x1`, `0x1/0xff`, or a plain number. This is how a port, a user or an application reaches the policy database — something marks, and this matches.

iif.title: iif
iif.description: Match packets that arrived on this interface. Names an interface of this device (`NG-F021`).

oif.title: oif
oif.description: Match packets that would leave by this interface — locally originated traffic from a socket bound to it. Names an interface of this device (`NG-F021`).

dscp.title: dscp
dscp.description: Match this DSCP code point, 0-63 (RFC 2474 §3) — the six bits, not the whole octet.

invert.title: invert
invert.description: Match everything the selectors do *not*. Needs a selector to invert (`NG-F017`).

action.title: action
action.description: What happens to a matching packet: `lookup` routes it by `table`, `blackhole`, `unreachable` and `prohibit` discard it, `goto` jumps to another priority. Default `lookup`.

table.title: table
table.description: The table to route by. Required by `lookup` and refused by every other action (`NG-F016`); names an entry of `spec.route_tables`, a VRF, or a reserved table (`NG-F019`).

goto.title: goto
goto.description: The priority to jump to. Required by `goto` and refused by every other action (`NG-F016`), and strictly greater than this rule's own — the database is walked upwards, so a backwards jump is a loop.

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the rule is for.

PolicyRule.title: PolicyRule

PowerConfig.description:
`spec.power` — a device's power, both directions (§17.2).

"Both directions" is the whole shape of it. A switch *takes* power through
`inputs` and *gives* it through `poe_budget_watts` and the `poe` blocks
on its ports; an access point takes power over its uplink and gives none. One
block covers all three because they are one question — where does the power
in this box come from and go to — and splitting it would put two halves of
one answer in two places.

draw_watts.title: draw_watts
draw_watts.description:
What the device draws. A bare number is the typical draw; a mapping states `typical` and optionally `maximum`.

YANG: `/eo-mib:eoPowerTable/eoPowerEntry/eoPower`

inputs.title: inputs
inputs.description:
One entry per power supply, naming the PDU outlet feeding it. At most 8. Empty for a device fed over PoE, or one whose feed is not recorded yet (`NG-E016`).

YANG: `/eo-ctx-mib:eoPowerRelationTable/eoPowerRelationEntry`

redundant.title: redundant
redundant.description: The feeds are meant to be independent: losing one must not lose the device. Needs at least two `inputs` (`NG-E002`) that land on different units and different feeds (`NG-E015`).

powered_by.title: powered_by
powered_by.description: Where the device's own power comes from: `outlet` (the default) or `poe`, meaning it takes power over its uplink and declares no `inputs` (`NG-E005`, `NG-E014`).

poe_budget_watts.title: poe_budget_watts
poe_budget_watts.description:
The PoE power this device can hand out across every PSE port together. `NG-E013` checks the ports that hold budget fit inside it.

YANG: `/power-ethernet-mib:pethMainPseTable/pethMainPseEntry/pethMainPsePower`

PowerConfig.title: PowerConfig

PowerDraw.title: power draw
PowerDraw.description: What the device draws, in watts. A bare number is the typical draw; the mapping form states `typical` and optionally `maximum`.

PowerInput.description:
One entry of `spec.power.inputs` — one PSU and the outlet feeding it.

Accepts the compact string form `pdu-r1-a:7` and the equivalent mapping
form, the same grammar a cable endpoint uses (§4.2), because it is the same
kind of fact: a named thing on a named element. `psu` labels the supply on
the *device* side, which is what an operator reads off the back of a chassis
and what makes a diagnostic about "the second input" name something real.

pdu.title: pdu
pdu.description: The PDU feeding this supply. An element reference, so it may be written fully qualified to pick one of several PDUs sharing a short name (`NG-E011`).

outlet.title: outlet
outlet.description: The outlet on it, as the PDU numbers it. Must exist (`NG-E011`) and must not already feed something else (`NG-E010`). Writable as the shorthand `pdu-r1-a:7`.

psu.title: psu
psu.description: Which supply on the device this feeds, e.g. `psu1`. Documentation only, and worth writing: it is what an operator reads off the back of a chassis.

PowerInput.title: PowerInput

PowerSource.description: Where a device's own power comes from (§17.2).
PowerSource.title: PowerSource

Protocol.description:
The IP protocol a rule selects on.

A closed set rather than a number, because the eight here are the ones a
policy is ever written about and a bare protocol number in a firewall rule is
almost always a typo for one of them. `icmp` and `icmpv6` are separate
protocols carried by separate families, which is a fact the schema can check
(`NG-B005`) only because they are not one entry called "icmp".
Protocol.title: Protocol

RadioRole.description:
§6.2.6 — which side of an association a radio is on.

`ap` beacons, so it is the end that owns the SSIDs; `station` and
`mesh` associate to one. A mesh node's backhaul radio is a station of the
node above it, spelled separately because it is a relay rather than a client
and a diagram should not draw it as a laptop.
RadioRole.title: RadioRole

RouteTable.description:
One entry of `spec.route_tables` — a routing table of its own (§16.3).

A table is a name and a number and nothing else, because that is all a table
is: a container routes are placed in. What makes it *do* anything is a policy
rule that looks it up (§16.4) — a table nothing selects holds routes nothing
consults, which is `NG-F023`.

The three tables every stack already has — `main`, `local` and
`default` — are never declared here and always nameable anyway; declaring
either their name or their number is `NG-F015`, because a second `main`
is not a second table, it is a document that has stopped describing the
device.

name.title: name
name.description: Name of the routing table. Unique within the device, and not one of the reserved `main`, `local` or `default`, which exist without being declared (`NG-F015`).

id.title: id
id.description: The number the table is known by, 1-4294967295. Unique within the device, and not 253, 254 or 255 — those are the reserved three under another name (`NG-F015`).

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the table is for.

RouteTable.title: RouteTable

`open` covers both a genuinely open network and OWE: netgraph records
whether a passphrase or an authentication server is involved, which is what
a reader of a diagram needs, and not the cipher suite negotiated on top.

StaticRoute.description:
One entry of `spec.routes` — a configured route (RFC 8349 `rt:route`).

A route needs somewhere to send the packet, so at least one of `via`,
`dev` and `blackhole` is required (`NG-F004`); `blackhole` excludes
the other two, because a route that discards has no egress.

prefix.title: prefix
prefix.description:
Destination prefix, either family, in canonical CIDR form. Host bits are rejected: a destination with them set is a typo or a host route, and netgraph will not guess which.

YANG: `…/rt:static-routes/v4ur:ipv4/v4ur:route/v4ur:destination-prefix`

via.title: via
via.description:
Next-hop address. Same family as `prefix` (`NG-F003`), and on a prefix the device configures (`NG-F008`).

YANG: `…/v4ur:route/v4ur:next-hop/v4ur:next-hop-address`

dev.title: dev
dev.description:
Egress interface, for an unnumbered next hop or a route pointed at an interface. Names an interface of this device (`NG-F009`).

YANG: `…/v4ur:route/v4ur:next-hop/v4ur:outgoing-interface`

vrf.title: vrf
vrf.description:
The routing instance holding the route. Names an entry of `spec.vrfs` (`NG-F005`); unset means the global instance.

YANG: `/ni:network-instances/ni:network-instance/ni:name`

table.title: table
table.description: The routing table holding the route; `main` when unset. Names an entry of `spec.route_tables` or a reserved table (`NG-F019`). A VRF is a table of its own, so `vrf` and `table` are alternatives, not a pair (`NG-F018`).

metric.title: metric
metric.description: Administrative distance or cost, as this device counts it. Documentation only: netgraph does not compute a best path.

blackhole.title: blackhole
blackhole.description:
Discard matching packets. Excludes `via` and `dev` (`NG-F004`).

YANG: `…/v4ur:route/v4ur:next-hop/v4ur:special-next-hop`

StaticRoute.title: StaticRoute

Style.description:
`spec.style` — the appearance of one element (§22).

Every field is optional and an absent one inherits; see the module
docstring for the ladder and `docs/styling.md` for the worked examples.

fill.title: fill
fill.description: Interior colour: a named colour or `#rrggbb`. `none` draws an unfilled shape.

stroke.title: stroke
stroke.description: Outline colour, and — on a cable or a tunnel — the colour of the line itself.

strokeWidth.title: strokeWidth
strokeWidth.description: Outline width in points, greater than 0 and at most 20.

dash.title: dash
dash.description: Line pattern: `solid`, `dashed`, `dotted` or `bold`. `bold` is a width rather than a pattern, spelled as Graphviz spells it because the built-in palette already is.

fontSize.title: fontSize
fontSize.description: Label size in points, between 6 and 96.

shape.title: shape
shape.description: The glyph the node is drawn as. Ignored on a cable or a tunnel, which has no shape.

anyOf.description: A picture in the icon theme, or 'none' for a plain shape.

icon.title: icon
icon.description: Picture to draw this one element as, overriding what the `--icons` theme picks for its kind. A bare name resolved inside the theme directory; `none` draws the plain shape.

opacity.title: opacity
opacity.description: How opaque the element is drawn, from 0 (invisible) to 1.

Template.description: A named partial device spec. A template declares no element: it is never drawn, never listed and never validated on its own. It exists to be merged into the devices that name it in `spec.from`, and the only place it surfaces is as the source location of a field it contributed.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. A named partial device spec, merged into every device that names it in `spec.from`. Not an element: never drawn, never listed, never validated on its own.

Template.title: Template

TemplateSpec.description: A partial device spec. Every key of a device `spec` is allowed and none is required: what the template does not say, the device using it says. `interfaces` is where the leverage is — one `range` entry is a whole line card.

vendor.title: vendor
vendor.description: Hardware vendor, free text. Documentation only.

serial.title: serial
serial.description: Serial or asset number, free text.

location.title: location
location.description: Physical location, free text (site, room, rack unit).

interfaces.title: interfaces
interfaces.description:
Every port and logical interface the device owns. At least one is required.

YANG: `/if:interfaces/if:interface`

bridge.title: bridge
bridge.description:
The 802.1Q bridge component this device implements. Absent means the device is not a bridge.

YANG: `/dot1q:bridges/dot1q:bridge`

vlans.title: vlans
vlans.description:
The device VLAN database: which VLANs exist on this device, and what they are called.

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-vlan/dot1q:vlan`

forwarding.title: forwarding
forwarding.description: Device-wide default for per-interface IP forwarding. Defaults to true/true on a `router` and false/false on every other kind; a `hub` must not declare it.

netns.title: netns
netns.description: The network namespaces this machine runs (§23.1). Each is a whole second network stack — its own interfaces, addresses and routing table — and `parent` nests one inside another, arbitrarily deep. Not a VRF: a VRF partitions one stack's routing table, a namespace *is* a second stack.

vrfs.title: vrfs
vrfs.description:
The routing instances (VRFs) this device implements. An interface binds to one with `vrf`, and that binding is what partitions the address namespace.

YANG: `/ni:network-instances/ni:network-instance`

route_tables.title: route_tables
route_tables.description: The routing tables this device holds beyond `main`, `local` and `default`. A table on its own changes nothing; what reaches it is a rule in `routing_policy` (§16.4).

routes.title: routes
routes.description:
Configured static routes, in the order the device holds them.

YANG: `…/rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/rt:control-plane-protocol/rt:static-routes`

routing_policy.title: routing_policy
routing_policy.description: The routing policy database: the ordered rules deciding which *table* a packet is routed by, from its source, its firewall mark, its ingress interface or its DSCP. This is policy-based routing (§16.4).

routing.title: routing
routing.description:
The dynamic routing protocols the device takes part in: an OSPF area, a BGP autonomous system, or both.

YANG: `…/rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/rt:control-plane-protocol`

zones.title: zones
zones.description: The security zones the device divides its interfaces into (§24.1). Policy is written *between* zones rather than between interfaces, so a rule survives a port being renamed, doubled or moved to a LAG. An interface is in at most one zone (`NG-B003`).

firewall.title: firewall
firewall.description: What the device does to the packets it sees: the filter policy and the address translations (§24.2). Absent records nothing about its filtering, which is not the same as saying it filters nothing.

power.title: power
power.description:
What the device draws, which PDU outlets feed it, and how much PoE it hands out (§17.2). Absent means the inventory records nothing about its power.

YANG: `/eo-mib:eoPowerTable/eoPowerEntry`

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

from.title: from
from.description: Names a `kind: template` document whose partial spec is merged underneath this one. The device's own keys win; `interfaces` merge by `name`; any other list the device declares replaces the template's outright. Resolved with the ordinary reference rules, so a template may live in another namespace (`templates/c9200l-48p`).

Unlike every other kind it is not applied by being in the tree: a rendering styles itself with the one `--theme` names, and this is only checked here.

spec.title: spec
spec.description: The body of a `theme` document: the styling rules, in declaration order. A theme is not applied by being in the tree — a rendering styles itself with the one `--theme` names — so this is checked here and used there.

Which elements one theme rule applies to (§22.3).

Every declared clause must hold. An empty selector matches everything.

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. An undirected logical link between two or more `tunnel` interfaces. Owns no interfaces; `over` nests it inside another tunnel.

Tunnel.title: Tunnel

TunnelAuth.description:
`spec.auth` — how the two ends prove who they are.

Deliberately an *enumeration of methods*, never a place to put material: a
key, a password or a certificate in an inventory is a secret in version
control, and netgraph has no use for one.
TunnelAuth.title: TunnelAuth

type.title: type
type.description: The encapsulation: `wireguard`, `ipsec`, `openvpn`, `pptp`, `l2tp`, `gre`, `vxlan` or `geneve`. It decides the layer carried, the outer transport, the default port, whether the payload is encrypted and how much MTU the headers cost.

endpoints.title: endpoints
endpoints.description: Two or more `device:interface` references, each naming an interface of `type: tunnel` (`NG-T001`, `NG-T003`). The link is undirected, so the list is sorted on load. Three or more endpoints make it multipoint, and it is then drawn as a node rather than a line.

over.title: over
over.description: The tunnel this one is encapsulated in — `vxlan` over `ipsec` is written by naming the IPsec tunnel here (`NG-T004`). Absent means the tunnel runs directly over the physical topology. The chain must not loop (`NG-T005`).

mode.title: mode
mode.description: IPsec's encapsulation mode, `tunnel` or `transport` (RFC 4301). Defaults to `tunnel`; every other type has only one mode and must not declare it (`NG-T008`).

vni.title: vni
vni.description: The 24-bit VXLAN/Geneve virtual network identifier. Required for those two types and rejected for every other (`NG-T007`).

port.title: port
port.description: Outer UDP/TCP port. Defaults to the registered port of the type (WireGuard 51820, OpenVPN 1194, L2TP 1701, VXLAN 4789, Geneve 6081) and is rejected for GRE and IPsec, which run directly over IP (`NG-T008`).

mtu.title: mtu
mtu.description: MTU of the tunnel interface. Compared with what the underlay leaves after the encapsulation overhead of the whole stack (`NG-T011`).

encrypted.title: encrypted
encrypted.description: Whether the payload is protected. Defaults to what the type does — true for WireGuard, IPsec and OpenVPN, false for GRE, VXLAN, Geneve, L2TP and PPTP, whose MPPE is broken. Set it to true to record that the deployment protects an otherwise cleartext type some other way.

cipher.title: cipher
cipher.description: Negotiated cipher suite, free text (`chacha20-poly1305`, `aes-256-gcm`). Only on a tunnel that encrypts (`NG-T009`).

auth.title: auth
auth.description: How the endpoints authenticate each other: `psk`, `certificate`, `public-key` or `password`. The *method*, never the material — netgraph stores no secrets (`NG-T010`).

label.title: label
label.description: Free-text identifier printed on the edge, as a cable's `label` is.

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

UpstreamPort.description: `spec.upstream` — the host-facing port of an adapter (§8.1).

name.title: name
name.description:
Name of the host-side port. Shares the interface namespace of the adapter (`NG-X004`) and may be named by a cable endpoint.

YANG: `/if:interfaces/if:interface/if:name`

type.title: type
type.description:
The host bus. `usb` and `usb-c` export as `ianaift:usb`; everything else as `ianaift:other`, because IANA registers no Thunderbolt or PCIe identity.

YANG: `…/if:type`

anyOf.title: Bit rate
anyOf.description: A link rate, either a whole number of bit/s or `<number><unit>` with unit `bps`, `kbps`, `Mbps`, `Gbps` or `Tbps` (`1Gbps`). Stored in bit/s.

speed.title: speed
speed.description:
Host-bus rate, e.g. `5Gbps` for USB 3.0. Written as bit/s or with a unit suffix.

YANG: `…/if:speed`

attached_to.title: attached_to
attached_to.description: The host the adapter is plugged into. A bare device name, never a `device:interface` reference (`NG-X001`). This is what joins the adapter to the graph when no cable does.

UpstreamPort.title: UpstreamPort

User.description: One identity: a person, a service account or a shared login (§19.1).

apiVersion.title: apiVersion
apiVersion.description: Schema version of the document. Only `netgraph.dev/v1alpha1` is understood by this release; an unknown value is `NG-D002`.

kind.title: kind
kind.description: Selects the shape of `spec`. One identity: a person, a service account or a shared login. Owns no interfaces and terminates no cable; it is drawn only in the `identity` view.

User.title: User

login.title: login
login.description:
The account name, when it differs from `metadata.name`; absent means the two are the same. Estate-wide, so two users claiming one login is `NG-S013`.

YANG: `/ietf-system:system/authentication/user/name`

full_name.title: full_name
full_name.description: The person's name as they write it. Free text: a real name is not a grammar.

email.title: email
email.description: Where mail reaches them, `local@domain.tld`. Also what ties the identity to a directory without netgraph having to model the directory.

uid.title: uid
uid.description:
POSIX user id, when the estate assigns one. 0 to 4294967294; two users claiming one is `NG-S013`.

YANG: `/ietf-system:system/authentication/user`

type.title: type
type.description: `person`, `service` or `shared`. Decides whether `NG-S015` and `NG-S016` have anything to say: only a person can depart, and only a person is expected in a group.

status.title: status
status.description: `active`, `suspended` or `departed`. A departed account is kept rather than deleted so the memberships still to be revoked stay visible (`NG-S015`).

ssh_keys.title: ssh_keys
ssh_keys.description:
Public keys the account authenticates with, `<algorithm> <base64> [comment]`. Normalised to single spaces; a private key is refused (`NG-S002`).

YANG: `/ietf-system:system/authentication/user/authorized-key`

style.title: style
style.description: How this element is drawn (§22): fill, stroke, shape, icon and five more. Every field is optional, and an absent one inherits from the theme, then the icon set, then the built-in palette.

UserStatus.description: Whether the account should still work (§19.1).
UserStatus.title: UserStatus

UserType.description:
What sort of account an identity is (§19.1).

The distinction is not cosmetic: three of the rules in the `S` group only
make sense for one of these. A service account belongs to no group in a great
many estates and reporting that as an oversight (`NG-S016`) would be noise;
a shared account has no single person to depart, so `NG-S015` has nothing
to say about it.

ViewGeometry.description: Everything one layer's drawing places, keyed by address.

mode.title: mode
mode.description: Access or trunk. 802.1Q has neither concept; netgraph expands the mode into a PVID, an acceptable-frame filter and VLAN membership (see docs/yang-mapping.md).

access_vlan.title: access_vlan
access_vlan.description:
The VLAN an access port belongs to, and the encapsulation VID of a `type: vlan` sub-interface. Required in access mode — it defaults to 1 — and forbidden in trunk mode (`NG-V002`).

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-port/dot1q:pvid`

trunk_vlans.title: trunk_vlans
trunk_vlans.description:
The tagged VLAN set of a trunk port. Required in trunk mode, forbidden in access mode.

YANG: `…/dot1q:vlan/dot1q:egress-ports (tagged)`

native_vlan.title: native_vlan
native_vlan.description:
The untagged VLAN on a trunk. Trunk mode only (`NG-V003`); it is implicitly a member of the port's VLAN set.

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-port/dot1q:pvid`

ingress_filtering.title: ingress_filtering
ingress_filtering.description:
Drop frames tagged with a VLAN the port is not a member of.

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-port/dot1q:enable-ingress-filtering`

acceptable_frames.title: acceptable_frames
acceptable_frames.description:
Which frames the port admits. Derived from `mode` and `native_vlan` when not stated.

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-port/dot1q:acceptable-frame`

VlanDefinition.description: One entry of `spec.vlans` — the device VLAN database (§6.4).

id.title: id
id.description:
VLAN identifier. Unique within the device (`NG-V001`).

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-vlan/dot1q:vlan/dot1q:vid`

name.title: name
name.description:
Human name of the VLAN. 802.1Q caps it at 32 characters.

YANG: `…/dot1q:bridge-vlan/dot1q:vlan/dot1q:name`

description.title: description
description.description: Free text. netgraph-only; 802.1Q has no such node.

VlanDefinition.title: VlanDefinition

VlanSet.title: VLAN set
VlanSet.description: A set of VLAN ids: a single id (`10`), a list (`[10, 20]`), a comma-separated string with ranges (`"10,20,100-110"`), or the keywords `all` (1-4094) and `none`. Normalised to the coalesced string form on load.

VrfDefinition.description:
One entry of `spec.vrfs` — a routing instance (RFC 8529 §4).

The name is how everything else refers to the instance: an interface binds
to it, a route is placed in it, and the address-collision rules partition
their namespace by it. Two devices that use the same name are taken to mean
the same VRF, which is what an operator means by "the blue VRF" — the route
distinguisher is recorded because MPLS needs it, not because netgraph
identifies the instance by it.

name.title: name
name.description:
Name of the routing instance. Unique within the device (`NG-F001`), and what an interface's `vrf` and a route's `vrf` refer to. Two devices using one name mean one VRF.

YANG: `/ni:network-instances/ni:network-instance/ni:name`

rd.title: rd
rd.description: Route distinguisher, in one of the three RFC 4364 §4.2 encodings: `65000:1`, `192.0.2.1:1` or `4200000000:1`. Quote it — an unquoted `65000:1` is a number to YAML.

description.title: description
description.description:
Free text: what the instance is for.

YANG: `/ni:network-instances/ni:network-instance/ni:description`

VrfDefinition.title: VrfDefinition

WirelessConfig.description:
`interfaces[].wireless` — the radio configuration of a `wifi` port.

Only a `wifi` interface may carry it (`NG-W002`): the block is what
turns an otherwise shapeless `medium: wireless` link into an association
with a direction, a frequency and a name.

role.title: role
role.description:
Which side of the association this radio is: `ap` beacons the SSIDs, `station` and `mesh` associate to one. A wireless link joins exactly one `ap` to one client (`NG-W007`).

YANG: `…/dot11:station-config/dot11:desired-bss-type`

band.title: band
band.description:
The band the radio operates in: `2.4GHz`, `5GHz` or `6GHz`. Required alongside `channel` and `width_mhz`, because both mean different frequencies in different bands.

YANG: `…/dot11:phy/dot11:channel-starting-factor`

channel.title: channel
channel.description:
The primary 20 MHz channel, as the band numbers it (`NG-W003`).

YANG: `…/dot11:phy/dot11:current-channel-number`

width_mhz.title: width_mhz
width_mhz.description:
Total channel width in MHz. 40 is the most 2.4 GHz can bond and 320 is 6 GHz only (`NG-W004`).

YANG: `…/dot11:phy/dot11:current-channel-width`

tx_power_dbm.title: tx_power_dbm
tx_power_dbm.description:
Radiated power in dBm. The MIB counts abstract power *levels* per PHY, so the unit is netgraph's own.

YANG: `…/dot11:phy/dot11:current-tx-power-level`

bss.title: bss
bss.description:
The basic service sets this radio beacons (`ap`) or is associated to (`station`, `mesh`, at most one — `NG-W006`).

YANG: `…/dot11:bss`

WirelessConfig.title: WirelessConfig

Zone.description:
One entry of `spec.zones` — a security zone (§24.1).

A name and the interfaces in it. The interfaces are what make the zone a
fact about the device rather than a label: policy is written between zones,
and which zone a packet is in is decided by the interface it crossed.

An interface belongs to at most one zone (`NG-B003`), and a zone holding no
interface at all is inert (`W150`) — nothing can be in it, so no rule
naming it can ever match.

name.title: name
name.description: Name of the zone. Unique within the device, and not `local`, which is the machine itself and is nameable in a rule without being declared (`NG-B001`).

interfaces.title: interfaces
interfaces.description: The interfaces in this zone. Each names an interface of this device (`NG-B002`), and no interface is in two zones (`NG-B003`). A zone holding none is inert (`W150`).

description.title: description
description.description: Free text: what the zone is for.

Zone.title: Zone
